source: Choi et al. (2026) Do multi-agent LLMs explore each other? (MACE)
finding: In a two-peer delegation bandit, LLM agents lock onto one peer within the first rounds. Choices are bimodal (near 0 or near 50 of 50), unlike UCB. This holds for Qwen2.5-7B and GPT-5.
numbers: 30 runs of T=50 rounds each; success rates (pA,pB)=(0.6,0.5); models include Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, GPT-4, GPT-5.
quote: LLM agents commit prematurely to one peer within the first few rounds
limits: Arithmetic delegation toy task; peers are fixed-probability. Preprint v3.
agent_relevance: Shows exploitation-only collapse in single agents; a program-set explore/exploit split (our G1 style) is the fix, not a prompt.

source: Choi et al. (2026) Do multi-agent LLMs explore each other? (MACE)
finding: Telling the model to balance exploration and exploitation in-context can do worse than random peer choice. Algorithmic structure (MACE) fixes it.
numbers: Figure 4: under contextual diversity (HotpotQA) In-Context Exploration had higher cumulative regret than Random; MACE lower. Gains persisted after exploration was switched off and transferred to 2WikiMultiHopQA. Seven models, four families, three benchmarks.
limits: Regret numbers are in figures; effect varies with peer heterogeneity.
agent_relevance: Supports G1: do not ask the model to self-balance; let code allocate exploration.

source: Choi et al. (2026) Do multi-agent LLMs explore each other? (MACE)
finding: Ablation of who computes the exploration rule: prompt only, formula in prompt, external calculator, pure algorithm.
numbers: Qwen-7B, pA=0.6 vs pB=0.4. Inferior-peer lock-in: prompt-only 50.0%, UCB formula in prompt 23.3%, LLM + external UCB scores 0.0%, algorithmic UCB 0.0%. Cumulative regret 20.0, 13.5, 9.9, 9.8.
limits: One small model, one task, small N.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence for code-computed counts with the LLM as slot-filler: calculator condition matched pure UCB.

source: Choi et al. (2026) Do multi-agent LLMs explore each other? (MACE)
finding: Even the strongest model concentrates on an early favourite among many peers.
numbers: GPT-5 selected Qwen-7B in 294 of 297 interactions.
limits: Single reported example; heterogeneous pool.
agent_relevance: Early-favourite lock-in is a real failure for any agent choosing among sub-strategies.

source: Choi et al. (2026) Do multi-agent LLMs explore each other? (MACE)
finding: Theory: MACE contextual-bandit peer selection has sublinear expected regret, while greedy empirical-mean selection can incur linear regret. With homogeneous peers (same LLM) gains are small.
numbers: MACE regret about O(sqrt(T log T)) under linear realizability; greedy Omega(T) on a constructed instance. Homogeneous-LLM setting: regret trends close to the random baseline.
limits: Proof under strong assumptions (linear, realizable).
agent_relevance: If sub-agents are copies of one model (G4), little to gain from exploring among them.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Out of all prompt and model configurations tested on multi-armed bandits, only one explored robustly: GPT-4 with chain-of-thought plus externally summarised history.
numbers: Models GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama2; many prompt designs. GPT-4 basic prompt (T=500, N=20) had suffix failures in more than 60% of replicates, like Greedy.
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior
limits: Simple MAB; authors say external summaries may be impossible in complex settings.
agent_relevance: Counts and summaries must be supplied by code (our rule), not left to model memory.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Second failure mode: the LLM behaves uniformly, picking all arms near-equally and failing to narrow down. The one success config matched Thompson Sampling.
numbers: Successful config: GPT-4, suggestive framing, summarised history, CoT, T=200, N=40; unimodal plays of best arm, very few suffix failures, reward comparable to TS.
limits: Qualitative failure taxonomy; temperature and prompt specific.
agent_relevance: Both too little (lock-in) and too much (uniform) exploration occur; need a controller.

source: Harris and Slivkins (2026) Should you use your LLM to explore or exploit? (UAI 2026)
finding: Silo study of LLMs as exploit oracles and as explore oracles in contextual bandits. Reasoning models exploit best; non-reasoning models need tool use or summaries; all LLMs lose to simple linear regression.
numbers: Models GPT-5.2, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Qwen-2.5, Gemma-3, Mistral-7B, DeepSeek-R1-distill. Text-based non-linear puzzle: linear regression baseline only 70% FracCorrect, yet all LLM configs still lost to it.
limits: Small puzzles; reasoning models slow (one experiment about $70 and 6+ hours).
agent_relevance: A structural split exploit versus explore is a testable design; use the LLM only where it adds semantics.

source: Harris and Slivkins (2026) Should you use your LLM to explore or exploit? (UAI 2026)
finding: In-context summaries rescue exploitation at large history. k-nearest and k-means summaries lifted accuracy but depended on hyper-parameters.
numbers: CB puzzle d=K=2, T=4000, GPT-4: without CoT all three mitigations reach about 80-90% FracCorrect; with CoT about 60-85%. d=K=5, T=1000, GPT-4o: k-means almost as bad as random, k-nearest about 50%, k-means with fewer centroids about 60%.
limits: Mitigations help on medium tasks only. CoT lowered scores in the K=d=2 case.
agent_relevance: Summaries help, CoT can hurt: consistent with doubt-only-on-signal (G1).

source: Harris and Slivkins (2026) Should you use your LLM to explore or exploit? (UAI 2026)
finding: LLMs are useful explore oracles: they propose candidates from large semantic action spaces that a bandit then tests.
numbers: MovieLens (943 users, 1682 movies): Qwen-2.5 average reward 671.88 (K=10) and 678.25 (K=19); Mistral-7B 735.38 and 675.16; Random 570.39 and 599.73; genre-based 617.27 (K=19). Telling the model to ignore popularity did not change rewards significantly.
limits: Tasks with semantic arms only; cosine-similarity reward on arXiv titles; model knowledge cutoff late 2023.
agent_relevance: Fits an ambidextrous split: LLM widens, program selects. Good fit for operator proposals.

source: Harris and Slivkins (2026) Should you use your LLM to explore or exploit? (UAI 2026)
finding: Asking for diverse candidates versus not, and all-at-once versus 1-by-1 generation, gave similar results.
numbers: All 4 prompting strategies performed similarly on the MovieLens explore puzzle. arXiv task, one category: K=1 0.63, K=5 0.68, MMR diversity baseline 0.40.
limits: Small effects; 10 abstract-title pairs per category.
agent_relevance: Prompted diversity is a weak lever; do not rely on it.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 on Wilson's horizon task: human-like in short horizon, but shows no directed exploration and ignores horizon for random exploration.
numbers: Short horizon regret indistinguishable from humans (t(5566)=-0.043, p=.97). Whole-task regret GPT-3 M=2.72 (SD 5.98) vs humans M=3.24 (SD 10.26), p<.001. Reward-difference effect beta=0.18, z=14.48 (random exploration); interaction with horizon beta=-0.02, p=.14; horizon effect on informative option beta=-0.15, p=.58.
limits: GPT-3 (2022), text-only horizon task; repeat bias partly from next-word training.
agent_relevance: The model could not time its exploration to remaining budget; pass budget remaining as explicit code state.

source: Bradley et al. (2023) Quality-diversity through AI feedback (QDAIF)
finding: An evolutionary archive (MAP-Elites) where an LM varies and judges both quality and diversity covers more of the space with good outputs than non-QD controls.
numbers: QD score significantly better than baselines in Opinions and Stories domains (5 seeds, bootstrap CI 100k resamples). Poetry: QDAIF 130 (CI 118-145) vs Random-Poems 76 (67-85) vs Fixed Seed Rewrite 99 (72-117).
limits: Creative writing; AI-human agreement only reasonable; not every domain showed a gap over the best baseline.
agent_relevance: Separate niches plus a quality filter is an LLM form of structural ambidexterity.

source: Lange, Imajuku and Cetin (2025) ShinkaEvolve
finding: Code-evolution agent with island subpopulations (structural separation), weighted parent sampling (exploit/explore balance) and novelty rejection. Beats AlphaEvolve circle packing with about 150 evaluations.
numbers: Circle packing n=26, sum of radii 2.635983, found in fewer than 150 program evaluations; ALE-Bench solutions improved by about 2.3%.
limits: Component ablations were run on one task (circle packing).
agent_relevance: Closest running example of structural ambidexterity in an LLM loop: islands plus migration.

source: Lange, Imajuku and Cetin (2025) ShinkaEvolve
finding: Ablation of parent choice: weighted sampling beats hill climbing and best-of-N.
numbers: Hill climbing started strong and plateaued; weighted sampling kept improving; random search worst. Shown in plots; score axis about 2.0 to 2.6.
limits: Curves only, no tabulated numbers.
agent_relevance: Pure exploitation stalls; a mixed rule wins. Supports balance, not either pole.

source: Lange, Imajuku and Cetin (2025) ShinkaEvolve
finding: Embedding-similarity novelty rejection helps; an extra LLM novelty judge adds little. Bandit LLM ensemble beat single LLM and fixed ensemble.
numbers: Proposals rejected above similarity 0.95. Single LLM baseline GPT-5-nano.
limits: Plots; text says significant but gives no tabulated values.
agent_relevance: Code-computed novelty filter beats judged novelty: matches our rule of code over opinion.

source: Lange, Imajuku and Cetin (2025) ShinkaEvolve
finding: Islands: independent subpopulations seeded alike, with occasional migration; the island-best program is blocked from migrating to protect uniqueness.
numbers: Config shows 2 to 4 islands and migration interval 10.
limits: No island-count ablation found in the text read.
agent_relevance: Explicit analogue of Gibson and Birkinshaw separate units with limited integration.

source: Wan et al. (2025) LoongFlow
finding: Multi-island MAP-Elites plus entropy-controlled Boltzmann selection: when population diversity falls, temperature rises to force exploration. Plan-Execute-Summarize loop.
numbers: Circle packing target 0.99: LoongFlow 258 evals on average vs OpenEvolve 783 (over 60% fewer); success 3/3 vs OpenEvolve 1/3; ShinkaEvolve 0/3 reached 0.99 (DeepSeek-R1-0528).
limits: Vendor paper (Baidu), 3 runs per arm, baselines rerun by authors.
agent_relevance: A signal-triggered switch between exploit and explore, as in G1.

source: Wan et al. (2025) LoongFlow
finding: Reports state-of-the-art on several AlphaEvolve suite problems with small margins.
numbers: Autocorrelation II 0.9027 vs AlphaEvolve 0.8962; circle packing radius 2.6359 vs 2.6358; hexagon side 3.92 vs 3.93 (lower is better).
limits: Some rows differ only in the 4th to 7th decimal; no confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Margins are small; treat as a hint.

source: Qian et al. (2025) Scaling LLM-based multi-agent collaboration (MacNet), ICLR 2025
finding: Org topology matters: irregular random networks of over a thousand agents beat regular ones, against human-org intuition. Different tasks prefer different shapes.
numbers: Random topologies took about 51.92% less time than mesh. Mesh beat tree beat chain on average. Chain suited software development, tree suited creative writing. Ablating agent profiles cut score by an average 3.67%. Majority voting added only 0.9%.
limits: Own benchmarks; open models showed a similar pattern; logistic collaborative scaling law reported.
agent_relevance: Fit structure to the task; extra voters add little (G4).

source: Georgiev, Gomez-Serrano, Tao and Wagner (2025) Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale
finding: AlphaEvolve run on 67 math problems rediscovered most best-known results and improved several.
numbers: 67 problems across analysis, combinatorics, geometry, number theory. Authors note diversity from cheaper models is powerful on many landscapes.
limits: Abstract and a few passages read; per-problem table not extracted.
agent_relevance: An explore-heavy LLM evolutionary loop works when a verifier exists (G3).

source: Atobishi and Nosratabadi (2026) Dynamic capabilities for AI-enabled exploration
finding: Survey of firms: sensing capability leads to AI-enabled exploration, which leads to innovation performance. AI-enabled exploration is a part of ambidexterity, not the whole.
numbers: N=245 senior executives in Saudi Arabia; PLS-SEM. AIE to innovation performance beta=0.604 (0.605 with controls; R2 0.365 to 0.397). Sensing to AIE beta=0.530. Government support to sensing beta=0.098, not significant. Competitive pressure moderates readiness to exploration (beta=0.151).
limits: Purposive sampling, one country, self-report; human firms using AI, not LLM behaviour.
agent_relevance: Human-org evidence only; adoption gains come via an exploration capability.

source: Atobishi and Nosratabadi (2026) Dynamic capabilities for AI-enabled exploration
finding: Cites He and Wong (2004): balancing exploration and exploitation outperforms either alone; ambidexterity defined by Raisch and Birkinshaw.
numbers: Secondhand; no figures in the text read.
limits: Not opened at source.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Boussaid et al. (2026) From replacement to orchestration: HARMONY
finding: Applies ambidexterity to agentic AI in R&D: automate routine work (exploitation), keep humans on abductive discovery (exploration).
numbers: Design-science paper; four expert interviews; scenario analysis. Cites GitClear: code churn up 39% in AI-heavy projects.
limits: Tiny N; conceptual; claim that agents cannot do abduction is asserted, not tested.
agent_relevance: Conceptual only; no test of an agent loop.

source: Tang, Zhao and Karahanna (2026) More than productivity? (AMCIS)
finding: Argues AI coding agents relieve the cognitive limits that force developers to trade exploration against exploitation.
numbers: Seen only as a search-result snippet; no numbers.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Conceptual claim to check later.
